items.prompt: An expense arrives with a well-formed body but a future date. Which layer rejects it, with which status?
distractors: DataAnnotations under [ApiController], as a malformed body: 400
The bearer-token authentication handler: 401
The [Authorize(Roles=...)] attribute on the action: 403
items.explanation: Shape problems are 400 from DataAnnotations; business rules such as 'no future date' are PolicyEngine flags answered with 422.

items.prompt: Approve carries [Authorize(Roles="Manager")]. Why does ExpenseService also call EnsureManagesOwner?
items.answer: The attribute only proves 'some manager'; the service check stops cross-team approvals
distractors: The attribute is skipped for API clients, so the service has to repeat the role check
EnsureManagesOwner refreshes the role claim if the token has expired
The service check only exists to write the approval into the audit history
items.explanation: Coarse attribute authorization is necessary but not sufficient; the resource check answers 'this manager manages this expense's owner'.

items.prompt: Someone adds UserRole.Auditor to the enum and nothing else. What can an Auditor see?
items.answer: Nothing: every role switch falls through to a deny arm
distractors: Everything an Employee can see, since that is the lowest existing role
Everything, because unknown roles are treated as administrators
Only their own expenses, via the owner-scoped GetOwned query
items.explanation: Every role switch has a `_ => false` / Enumerable.Empty arm: a new role gets no access until deliberately granted. The list of places to touch is the security surface.

items.prompt: Why can a blocking policy flag appear at submit time that was absent when the expense was created?
items.answer: Policy re-runs at create, update and submit on current data
distractors: Flags are only computed at submit; create and update skip the PolicyEngine entirely
The approver adds blocking flags by hand while reviewing the expense
A background job recalculates every flag nightly and stores the result
items.explanation: RefreshPolicy runs on each of the three operations; e.g. the stale-date warning depends on when it is evaluated.

items.prompt: How do Blocking and Warning flags from PolicyEngine differ in effect?
items.answer: Blocking flags stop submission; warnings travel with the expense to the approver
distractors: Blocking flags notify Finance; warnings are only written to the server log
Both stop submission, but the employee may override a warning
Warnings stop submission; blocking flags only show on the approver's screen
items.explanation: Rules include amount > 0, description present, no future date, receipt required over $25, per-category limits and a high-value warning.

items.prompt: The login path verifies a password hash to equalise timing, yet the guide calls that equalisation partial. Why?
items.answer: It still returns early when the user does not exist, so timing can differ
distractors: PBKDF2 with 100k iterations runs in variable time for different passwords
The constant-time comparison is only applied to the admin accounts
The salt is stored beside the hash, which leaks whether the user exists
items.explanation: PBKDF2 + per-user salt + constant-time compare is done right; the early return on a missing user is the gap to investigate.

items.prompt: In incident 001, money moved for expenses that were never approved. What single change caused it?
items.answer: A new Submitted -> Reimbursing edge for Finance in the ExpenseStateMachine table
distractors: The [Authorize(Roles = "Finance")] attribute was removed from the Reimburse action
The background job stopped checking the payment reference before paying
Approve lost its EnsureManagesOwner resource check in the service
items.explanation: The transition table is the sole authority and ExpenseService.Transition the only place status changes, so one dictionary entry was enough for an end-to-end bypass.

items.prompt: Why did the background job finish the fast-tracked reimbursements instead of catching them?
items.answer: It only checks Reimbursing -> Reimbursed is legal, not the path taken
distractors: It re-checks the approval history, but it reads from a stale cache
It runs with Finance's role, so the state machine always allows it
It retries until the provider accepts the payment, ignoring the state
items.explanation: CanSystemTransition(Reimbursing, Reimbursed) is legal regardless of path; once Finance fast-tracks, the worker stamps a PaymentReference.

items.prompt: The PR said it enabled 'pre-approved recurring vendor charges'. What should a reviewer have flagged?
items.answer: The (from, to, role) table cannot express the narrow vendor exception
distractors: The PR lacked a feature flag, so it shipped to every tenant at once
Recurring charges need a scheduled job, which the PR did not add
Vendor names were stored unvalidated in the free-text description
items.explanation: A narrow English description backing a table-driven change that has no way to express 'narrow' is the pattern to flag.

items.prompt: A postmortem proposes 'add authorization checks in the controller' as the fix for incident 001. How does the answer key judge that?
items.answer: Reasonable defense in depth, but not the root-cause fix: the state table was wrong
distractors: The correct root-cause fix, since the controller let Finance call Reimburse directly
Wrong, because controllers must never perform any authorization
Unnecessary, because the data-correction step already closes the hole
items.explanation: The Finance attribute was never wrong; remove the bad edge and also correct data for Reimbursed expenses with no Approved event.

items.prompt: Which first regression test does the answer recommend for the state machine?
items.answer: A table test pinning the complete set of legal (from, to, role) triples
distractors: An end-to-end UI test that clicks through approve and then reimburse
A load test proving the background job handles 1,000 expenses
A mock-based test asserting Transition calls the repository once
items.explanation: The repo had zero tests; a full-combination characterization test fails immediately on this diff and is cheap to keep green.

items.prompt: In incident 002, removing the extension-equality check was legitimate. What was the actual bug?
items.answer: The stored file's extension came from the client, not the allowlist
distractors: The Content-Type header was no longer validated at all
Uploaded files could escape the uploads folder through ../ paths
The GUID part of the stored file name became predictable
items.explanation: Content-Type is still checked against the allowlist, but the on-disk extension became attacker-controlled and decoupled from it.

items.prompt: Why is the receipt-extension mismatch called a latent risk rather than an exploit today?
items.answer: Downloads use the validated Content-Type; future extension-trusting code would break
distractors: The GUID base name stops anyone from ever opening the stored file by its URL
Path.GetExtension rejects .html and .svg names before the file is saved
The antivirus pipeline already sniffs the file bytes during every upload
items.explanation: It is not path traversal or overwrite; it is a broken invariant that a future static mount, CDN or extension-branching pipeline would make exploitable.

items.front: Describe dotnet-ramp's two-layer authorization model for expenses (reads and writes).
items.back: Coarse: [Authorize(Roles=...)] says 'some manager'. Fine: service checks such as EnsureManagesOwner, CanView/List scoping reads to own/team/all by role, and owner-scoped writes via GetOwned. The fine layer is the IDOR defense.

items.front: Incident 001 diagnostic path: where does a senior start, and why not the controller?
items.back: At the one documented place status changes (ExpenseService.Transition), then back to ExpenseStateMachine.CanTransition, then reading the Transitions table for any edge whose role disagrees with the diagram in the class doc comment.

items.front: What single regression test pins the receipt-storage invariant?
items.back: For Content-Type image/jpeg and an IFormFile named exploit.html, assert Receipt.StoredFileName ends in .jpg, never .html - it holds regardless of how the surrounding checks change.

items.front: Besides removing the bad edge, what does fixing incident 001 require, and why?
items.back: A data-correction step: find every Reimbursed expense with no Approved history event. It is a financial control and money already moved, so a code fix alone leaves bad records.
